problem_plain: Graphics chips were built to paint pixels on a screen, not to run AI models or protect secret data. Different kinds of work — keeping data encrypted while computing on it, controlling a quantum computer, guiding a robot, or drawing a 3D scene — each need a very different rhythm of computation. Some tasks are deeply step-by-step; some can do millions of things at once; some spend most of their time moving numbers around rather than doing arithmetic on them. No single chip design handles all of these well. This theme asks: when the job is so different from standard AI training that a graphics chip is the wrong tool entirely, what chip should you use instead?
why_plain: Each of these specialized tasks has a specific bottleneck that graphics chips are bad at. Computing on encrypted data inflates every number into a list thousands of entries long, so even simple addition floods the connection between the chip and its memory — long before the arithmetic parts of the chip break a sweat. Quantum computers need classical electronics to send precise pulses and read results back in millionths of a second; ordinary server software is far too slow. Robotics and 3D mapping flip back and forth between large organized calculations and highly scattered memory reads that neither general-purpose nor graphics chips handle gracefully. The common thread: the bottleneck is always moving data, not doing arithmetic.
approach_plain: Researchers respond by designing chips, compilers, and algorithms together — each piece shaped to eliminate the specific data-movement bottleneck of its domain. Three patterns repeat across papers: (1) place the arithmetic unit physically next to the data it needs, so the data never has to travel far; (2) redesign the algorithm so it produces less data in the first place; (3) build a chip that can reshape its internal wiring to match an irregular workload, rather than forcing the workload to fit a rigid pipeline.

groups.heading: Chips that compute on encrypted data
groups.explain: Normally, a server must decrypt your data before it can do anything with it — which means the server operator can read your secrets. A technique called Fully Homomorphic Encryption lets a server compute on data that stays scrambled the entire time. The catch is steep: each encrypted number secretly becomes a list of thousands of ordinary numbers, and even simple operations balloon into transfers of several megabytes. The chip's link to its memory fills up long before its arithmetic units are busy. The papers here attack this by moving arithmetic physically into the memory chips (so data never has to travel), by spreading work across many chips, by rewriting algorithms to reduce expensive steps, and by building compilers that automatically handle the periodic 'noise cleanup' step — a necessary reset that must happen after a certain number of multiplications, or the encrypted result becomes unreadable.

papers.name: FHENDI
papers.gloss: Places arithmetic units inside the memory chips themselves; a clever wiring scheme lets them do the butterfly-shaped sums that encrypted math requires, cutting average wait time 2145x versus a CPU.

papers.name: Anaheim
papers.gloss: Discovers that the real bottleneck in encrypted computing on a graphics chip is simple element-by-element modular addition, not the flashier transforms; moves just those additions into the memory chips.

papers.name: Cinnamon
papers.gloss: Spreads encrypted computation across many small chips stacked together instead of one giant chip; a matching compiler and reworked algorithm cut data traffic between chips, running an AI language task in 1.67 seconds versus 17 hours on a CPU.

papers.name: Hydra
papers.gloss: Distributes encrypted AI inference across multiple flexible-chip server cards using a pipeline where each card handles a different layer; 74 to 160 times faster than comparable single-card designs.

papers.name: WarpDrive
papers.gloss: Runs both the specialized matrix-math units and the general compute units on a graphics chip at the same time inside the same encrypted-math operation; lifts throughput 13.4x on a top data-center GPU.

papers.name: Neo
papers.gloss: Rewrites the polynomial arithmetic at the heart of encrypted computing as matrix multiplications so the graphics chip's built-in matrix-math units can accelerate it, with no new silicon required.

papers.name: EFFACT
papers.gloss: A complete encrypted-computing platform — compiler plus flexible and custom chip hardware — that streams data through small on-chip fast memory to maintain high throughput, and reuses circuit blocks to shrink chip area.

papers.name: FAST
papers.gloss: One chip that supports two different noise-cleanup algorithms and adjustable number precision, switching between them automatically based on how much noise budget the current encrypted value has left.

papers.name: ReSBM
papers.gloss: A compiler that uses a graph-cutting algorithm to find the fewest possible noise-cleanup resets a program needs, provably reducing the most expensive step in encrypted computing.

papers.name: HALO
papers.gloss: First compiler able to correctly place noise-cleanup resets inside program loops, making it possible to compile looping algorithms into encrypted computing automatically, without programmer intervention.

papers.name: CIPHERMATCH
papers.gloss: Redesigns encrypted text search to use only cheap additions instead of expensive multiplications, then adds a small compute unit inside the storage chip so encrypted data never has to travel to main memory at all.

Adds three new instructions to ordinary desktop-server CPUs that dramatically speed up the large-number transforms used in encrypted computing and post-quantum security; 38x faster than previous CPU code, nearly matching purpose-built chips.

groups.heading: Silicon for zero-knowledge proofs and privacy-preserving verification
groups.explain: A zero-knowledge proof is a mathematical certificate that lets one party convince another it ran a computation correctly — or knows a secret — without revealing any of the underlying data. Blockchains and verifiable AI use these proofs constantly, but generating one can take minutes on an ordinary computer because it requires enormous multiplications over very large numbers and aggregating thousands of points on a mathematical curve. Like encrypted computing, the bottleneck is data movement, but the internal structure of the math is different enough to need its own hardware.

papers.name: zkSpeed
papers.gloss: A purpose-built chip with eight dedicated units for one specific proof protocol; sharing multipliers across proof phases cuts chip area by 49%, and the whole chip is 801 times faster than a server CPU at generating proofs.

papers.name: LegoZK
papers.gloss: A flexible custom chip where one type of arithmetic unit handles every phase of proof generation by changing its internal connections at runtime; 32 times faster than the previous proof-generation chip at 37% lower power.

papers.name: UniZK
papers.gloss: A grid of multiply-add cells — like a small calculator array — extended with extra local connections and a mode for operating on whole lists at once, so one unified piece of silicon handles every type of proof operation; 97 times faster than a CPU.

papers.name: BatchZK
papers.gloss: A graphics-chip pipeline that overlaps successive proof-generation stages across many proofs at once, turning a step-by-step per-proof flow into a high-throughput batch; targets blockchain applications.

A multi-graphics-chip approach to the number-transform step at the heart of proof generation; restructures the butterfly-shaped computation to minimize data sent between chips, enabling proof generation to scale across many cards.

papers.name: Finesse
papers.gloss: A compiler and chip designed together for a specific class of cryptographic proof; a novel instruction scheduler eliminates pipeline stalls, reaching 34 times the throughput of a prior flexible design and 3 times that of a fixed-function chip.

groups.heading: Quantum computer control and compilation
groups.explain: A quantum chip is useless without fast classical electronics that send precise microwave or laser pulses, read back measurement results in millionths of a second, and feed those results into the next step — all before the fragile quantum state decays. Ordinary server software running on a general-purpose processor is too slow for this by a wide margin. Beyond control electronics, quantum programs need compilers that shrink the number of operations before the quantum state degrades. The papers here cover both: hardware that closes the feedback loop fast enough, and software that trims circuit size before running.

papers.name: Distributed-HISQ
papers.gloss: A control architecture where each controller announces its upcoming sync points in advance so others can prepare; eliminates round-trip waiting, cutting total program time by 22.8% and error rate by 5 times.

papers.name: Qtenon
papers.gloss: A standard open-source processor chip extended with quantum-specific instructions and a shared memory region between the classical and quantum processors; tight coupling cuts the delay in hybrid classical-quantum algorithms by 14.9 times.

papers.name: ARTERY
papers.gloss: Borrows the trick CPUs use to guess which branch a program will take — applied to quantum measurement results — so the controller acts on the most likely outcome before the answer arrives; 2 times lower feedback delay, 1.24 times better result quality.

A calibration method that measures each pair of quantum bits individually and runs non-interfering calibrations in parallel; reduces calibration time 8 to 25 times and cuts two-qubit gate error by 1.84 times.

papers.name: guoq
papers.gloss: A quantum circuit optimizer that alternates fast local rewrites with slower exhaustive search on the most promising small pieces, achieving stronger gate-count reductions than either technique could alone.

papers.name: QuCLEAR
papers.gloss: A quantum compiler that moves a whole class of simple gates — ones that can be simulated on a regular computer — to the end of the circuit and removes them via classical math, cutting entangling gate depth by up to 84%.

papers.name: HATT
papers.gloss: Builds the mapping from chemistry problems to qubit operations in a way tailored to each specific molecule's structure; 5 to 25% fewer gates than generic mappings.

papers.name: QR-Map
papers.gloss: Finds opportunities to measure and reset qubits mid-circuit and reuse them, using a fast map-based analysis that runs in polynomial time; 20% average qubit reduction, 25% circuit depth reduction.

papers.name: S-SYNC
papers.gloss: A compiler for trapped-ion quantum processors that jointly optimizes physically moving qubits and swapping their logical connections, rather than handling these separately; 3.69 times fewer physical moves, 1.73 times better success rate.

papers.name: SwitchQNet
papers.gloss: A compiler for quantum data centers that groups optical-switch reconfigurations from many operations together to spread the setup cost across all of them at once; 8 times lower communication latency.

papers.name: TQSim
papers.gloss: A noisy quantum circuit simulator that saves intermediate quantum states in a tree structure and reuses them across different noise trials rather than recomputing from scratch; up to 3.89 times faster on large computing clusters.

groups.heading: Quantum error correction hardware
groups.explain: Quantum information is fragile — stray electromagnetic fields constantly flip the state of quantum bits. Quantum error correction handles this by encoding one reliable 'logical quantum bit' across dozens or hundreds of physical ones, continuously measuring for signs of errors without reading the actual data, then figuring out what went wrong and fixing it. The decoder that identifies errors must finish before the next error arrives — within about one millionth of a second on today's hardware — which rules out software on a conventional processor. These papers build purpose-built decoders and memory layouts that make fault-tolerant quantum computing physically possible.

papers.name: Micro Blossom
papers.gloss: The first hardware implementation of the exact best-known matching algorithm for quantum error decoding; dedicates one small processing unit to each quantum bit and each possible error connection, running the hardest decoding step in programmable logic at 0.8 microseconds average.

papers.name: GLADIATOR
papers.gloss: Detects when a quantum bit has leaked into a higher energy level — a particularly damaging error — using only 10 logic steps per bit per cycle; 1.7 to 3.9 times fewer cycles wasted on leakage, 16% lower logical error rate.

papers.name: LSQCA
papers.gloss: Splits quantum memory into fast-access slots and a denser slower store; nearly doubles the usable quantum bit count at only a 5% slowdown by tolerating variable-latency access to stored qubits.

papers.name: HetEC
papers.gloss: Mixes two types of error-correcting codes — ones that are easy to build locally and ones that are far more efficient at large scale — in one architecture, getting universal computation with better overall resource use than either type alone.

A protocol for quantum network links that converts noisy shared quantum states into reliable ones at a steady, predictable rate regardless of noise, unblocking distributed quantum computing across machines.

groups.heading: Light-based and analog computing for specific domains
groups.explain: Light passing through a shaped optical region can perform a multiplication nearly for free — the physics of the lens does the arithmetic, using almost no energy. Analog chips — where a voltage level encodes a number rather than a binary 1 or 0 — similarly exploit physical laws to do in one step what would take many transistor operations digitally. Both approaches trade some flexibility and numerical precision for extreme energy efficiency in the narrow domains where they apply.

papers.name: LightML
papers.gloss: The first complete light-based AI accelerator system, including matched memory and data-routing designs that keep the optical core busy more than 80% of the time; delivers 325 trillion operations per second at 3 watts.

papers.name: RLGS
papers.gloss: A learning-based compiler that finds the best sequence of operations for creating entangled groups of light particles in a photonic quantum computer; 31 to 58% less generation time, 38 to 58% fewer error-prone operations.

papers.name: Fat-Tree QRAM
papers.gloss: A quantum memory design that handles multiple simultaneous read requests by duplicating routing nodes in a branching tree pattern; delivers constant memory bandwidth regardless of memory size, unlike earlier designs where bandwidth shrank as memory grew.

papers.name: DS-TPU
papers.gloss: An analog chip that learns from graph-structured data directly on-device using feedback electric current as a correction signal; 810 times faster than training the same task on a graphics chip, at 5 watts, with 10.8% better accuracy.

groups.heading: Flexible chips as adaptable accelerators
groups.explain: A flexible chip — one whose internal wiring can be changed in software rather than being fixed at manufacture — is attractive for workloads that evolve quickly or need specialized data routing without the cost of a fully custom chip. The challenge is that each model of flexible chip has a different internal structure, and connecting multiple flexible chips or sharing one among many users requires careful software layers. The papers here build those layers.

papers.name: RSN
papers.gloss: Treats the flexible chip as a switchable stream network rather than a sequential instruction processor; pipelines multiple AI model layers simultaneously without reprogramming, matching graphics chip latency at only 18% of the memory bandwidth.

papers.name: Nyx
papers.gloss: A virtualization layer that adds temporary holding buffers between pipelined tasks on a flexible chip, so dependent stages can run at different times on shared hardware; 1.26 to 8.87 times higher throughput over simple task-sharing.

papers.name: Harmonia
papers.gloss: A standard interface definition for cloud flexible chips that lets an accelerator design run on different chip models without modification, hiding hardware differences behind a common connection contract.

papers.name: IDEA-GP
papers.gloss: A flexible-chip accelerator for robot mapping algorithms that profiles the current task at runtime and dynamically schedules operations onto a shared compute array; 7.5 to 41.6 times faster than running the same task on a CPU.

groups.heading: Purpose-built chips for robotics, 3D scenes, and edge sensing
groups.explain: The final group covers tasks that are neither purely AI nor purely cryptographic but share the same root problem: memory access that jumps around unpredictably, mixed with computation that switches between large organized calculations and thinly scattered ones. Reconstructing a 3D scene, planning a robot's path, and streaming volumetric video all require processing thousands of geometric pieces per frame, with the relevant pieces changing unpredictably each time. Purpose-built chips or chip extensions handle this far more efficiently than general-purpose hardware.

papers.name: RTGS
papers.gloss: An algorithm and chip designed together for real-time 3D scene mapping using cloud-like blobs of color and opacity; 48.8 times faster than a small edge graphics chip at 82.5 times the energy efficiency.

papers.name: REACT3D
papers.gloss: An edge chip that continuously updates a 3D scene model from a live camera by predicting which scene blobs changed using spatial patterns and skipping the rest; 12 times faster and 33 times more energy-efficient than a standard edge AI board.

papers.name: GBU
papers.gloss: An add-on rendering unit for edge graphics chips that processes 3D scene blobs row by row, sharing intermediate values between neighboring pixels and skipping blobs below a contribution threshold; enables 60-plus frames per second AR/VR versus 7 to 17 on the baseline.

papers.name: Uni-Render
papers.gloss: A single reconfigurable chip that handles multiple different 3D scene-rendering algorithms by switching its internal data-flow pattern at runtime; up to 119 times faster than prior neural rendering hardware at 5 watts.

A graphics-chip ray-tracing accelerator that keeps far more rays active at once by releasing compute units after they fire their ray query, then reusing cached geometry data across the larger set of in-flight rays; 95% average speedup.

papers.name: HiPER
papers.gloss: A chip for robot navigation that alternates between running a neural network and running an optimization loop for motion planning; a branching wiring layout and multi-level scheduler handle the alternating dense-then-scattered compute pattern; 10.75 times faster than a gaming graphics chip.

papers.name: Pirate
papers.gloss: A VR streaming system that sends only one eye's view at a time and reconstructs the other eye's view on-device from depth differences; achieves 90 frames per second at bandwidths as low as 0.1 bits per pixel.

A cost model for computing satellites in low Earth orbit showing that using high-efficiency AI chips instead of commodity hardware reduces total ownership cost 116 times, despite a higher per-chip price.

papers.name: SMX
papers.gloss: A chip pairing a new CPU instruction extension for edge-case alignment with a 2D coprocessor for regular pattern matching; handles DNA, protein, and text alignment in 0.34 square millimeters of silicon, 256 to 744 times faster than software.

papers.name: BQSim
papers.gloss: A graphics-chip quantum circuit simulator that runs many input states at once using decision diagrams to find shared sub-calculations; 3.25 times faster than the standard GPU quantum simulator, 311 times faster than an open-source one.

papers.name: VoLUT
papers.gloss: A 3D volumetric video system that pre-computes a neural network's outputs into a lookup table once offline, then runs real-time video upscaling on a mobile phone using table lookups instead of running the network again.

papers.name: FedProphet
papers.gloss: A distributed training system that splits a large AI model into sequential pieces so memory-limited edge devices each train one slice; a central coordinator dynamically balances prediction accuracy against robustness to attacks.

papers.name: RISSP
papers.gloss: An automated method that builds minimal processors for bendable plastic-substrate chips by including only the instructions a given application actually uses; 40 times more energy-efficient per instruction than a small standard processor core.

Encodes a neural network's weights as signal delay times and its intermediate values as signal arrival times rather than binary numbers; 11 times better energy than spike-based networks, 3.5 times better than 8-bit digital arrays, while staying compatible with standard AI training tools.
Adds a matrix-math unit to an open-source graphics processor; multiple threads cooperate to share one matrix operation, reducing memory pressure; up to 3 times better utilization than the baseline.

connect: Every paper in this theme is fighting the same battle: the arithmetic itself is cheap, but moving the data to where the arithmetic happens is expensive, slow, or burns too much power. Encrypted-computing chips put arithmetic units inside the memory chips so ciphertext never has to travel across a wire. Quantum control chips sit microseconds away from the quantum bits to close the feedback loop in time. Edge rendering chips reuse cached scene geometry across pixels to avoid loading it again. The memory wall that slows down AI model inference is the same wall — just wearing a different face in each domain — and the answer is always the same: shrink the distance between where data lives and where arithmetic happens.
